newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea heavy industry sees 1H losses, rebound see.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea heavy industry sees 1H losses, rebound see.

text.p: South Korean heavy industry posted losses in the first half of calendar 1997 due to a slowdown in global shipbuilding and high finance burdens, but full-year earnings would improve, analysts said on Wednesday.

"Low profitability had been anticipated as first-half earnings reflected shipbuilding orders received in 1995 and 1996, when shipbuilders had to tolerate low ship prices," said Kim Hag-ju, shipbuilding analyst at Hyundai Securities.
Analysts said recently that improving vessel prices, the strengthening of the yen against the U.S. dollar and rising productivity would help South Korean shipbuilders later this year.
They said that despite the recent weakness of the yen to the dollar, the Japanese currency had in fact strengthened in the first half of this year compared with a year earlier.
They also expect the yen to make further gains in the second half. The yen was last trading at 116.50 to the dollar.
A big loss by Samsung Heavy Industries Co was the main reason the industry reported combined losses in the first six months.

Samsung Heavy, a machinery and shipbuilding affiliate of the Samsung Group, reported a 91.2-billion won net loss ($101.9-million) during the first six months, compared to a 7.4-billion won profit a year earlier.
Its turnover rose to 1.75 trillion won from 1.66 trillion a year earlier.
"Heavy investments in the past year to expand its dockyards left Samsung Heavy with very burdensome interest payments," said Lee Jong-seung, senior analyst at Daewoo Securities.
He said Samsung now has a capacity of two million gross tons (GT), up from 700,000 GT in 1993.
A one-million-GT capacity can accommodate construction of an oil tanker and a very large crude carrier (VLCC) at the same time, or four smaller vessels.
Analysts said Samsung had been hit by high financing costs following huge investments in its commercial vehicle unit.
Daewoo Heavy Industries Co, an affiliate of the Daewoo Group, posted 37.7 billion won in net profit in the first half, against 36.8 billion won in the year ago period.
Its sales totalled 2.83 trillion won in the first half, up from 2.5 trillion a year earlier.

"As for profitability, Daewoo Heavy is currently the most profitable, due to the good profitability of its minicar division and absence of major shipbuilding capacity expansion during the past few years," said Kang Hun-sok at ING Barings.

"We performed well in shipbuilding, some machinery and mini-cars," a director at Daewoo Heavy said. "With the economy improving in the second half, we believe we can meet our sales target of six trillion won this year."
Daewoo reported sales of 5.1 trillion won last year.
The six-month net of Hanjin Heavy Industry turned to a profit of 7.6 billion won from a 7.2-billion loss a year ago.
Analysts said orders of higher value-added container ships from its affiliate Hanjin Shipping Co helped the shipbuilder improve its profits for the first half.
"The worst is already over for the shipbuilders," said Han Kumhee at Merrill Lynch Securities.
"Orders to replace old VLCCs are rising, ship prices are rising and shipbuilders are enjoying increasing negotiating power as their docks become full," she said.
Analysts said a VLCC costs $80 million in the first quarter, but rebounded to $82-$83 million from April.
They said Samsung would break even or post a slight loss for all of 1997 against a 280-billion-won loss a year earlier.
"Contributions from container deliveries, significant declines in labour costs and raw material as a percentage of sales are expected," Han said.
Daewoo was forecast to post 70-to-80 billion won in net profit from a 74.7-billion won profit a year earlier.
